subsystems.name: Rotor (moving mass)
subsystems.role: a continuous stream of magnetically levitated pellets or a cable loop circling the planet faster than orbital speed, whose outward push holds everything up.

subsystems.name: Contained sheath
subsystems.role: the stationary tube the rotor runs inside, keeping it in vacuum and carrying the maglev guides.

subsystems.name: Magnetic suspension
subsystems.role: couples the fast rotor to the stationary tube without contact, transferring its outward force as lift.

subsystems.name: Outer platform
subsystems.role: the non-rotating structure the ring exists to carry: habitats, factories, launch rails.

subsystems.name: Anchor tethers
subsystems.role: passive cables hanging from the ring to fixed points on the surface, providing the mechanical path up and down.

subsystems.name: Power and control
subsystems.role: feeds energy into the rotor to make up losses and keeps a 40,000 km structure stable.

buildSteps.title: Establish low-orbit industry
buildSteps.detail: Build the launch capacity, orbital assembly robots and power supply needed to move thousands of tonnes of material into low Earth orbit.

buildSteps.title: Deploy a bootstrap loop
buildSteps.detail: Place a simple cable loop in low orbit at roughly 200–400 km altitude — small, unanchored and held only by its own orbital motion.

buildSteps.title: Spin it up
buildSteps.detail: Use linear motors, powered from the ground or from solar arrays, to accelerate the loop past orbital velocity so it starts pushing outward on its guides rather than falling freely.

buildSteps.title: Expand the ring
buildSteps.detail: As rotor speed rises, the loop climbs to a larger radius while remaining circular, growing into a full planet-circling ring.

buildSteps.title: Add the stationary sheath
buildSteps.detail: Build the non-rotating tube and maglev guides around the moving rotor, assembled in orbit from launched or space-mined material.

buildSteps.title: Anchor to the ground
buildSteps.detail: Lower tethers from the ring to surface stations near the equator; the ring's outward force tensions them, and the tethers in turn pin the ring's position.

buildSteps.title: Build the platform
buildSteps.detail: Attach the deck, habitats and electromagnetic launcher rails to the stationary sheath, one segment at a time.

buildSteps.title: Commission the transit system
buildSteps.detail: Run climbing cars up the tethers and fire payloads from the launcher rails, with the rotor continuously re-accelerated to replace losses.

prerequisites.why: the first loop must be launched from Earth; today's prices are far too high for thousands of tonnes.
nobody has assembled a structure thousands of kilometres long in space.
maglev trains and laboratory bearings exist, but not at the speeds and continuous duty a ring rotor needs.
a ring this large is flexible and would need continuous, millisecond-scale damping to avoid oscillations and failure.
the rotor loses energy to magnetic and radiation losses that must be continuously replaced.

pathway.milestone: reusable rockets driving launch costs down; orbital ring remains a theoretical concept studied since the 1980s
pathway.unlocks: a realistic path to moving bulk material into space.

pathway.milestone: orbital construction of large trusses, solar arrays and propellant depots
pathway.unlocks: the industrial base for a bootstrap loop.

pathway.milestone: a short, unanchored high-speed rotor loop tested in low orbit
pathway.unlocks: proof that active support and maglev work in vacuum over long spans.

pathway.milestone: a complete unanchored ring circling the planet
pathway.unlocks: cheap surface-to-orbit transport via tethers, without rockets.

pathway.milestone: full anchored platform with launch rails and habitation
pathway.unlocks: planetary-scale transit and a base for further megastructures — if economics and orbital debris control can be solved.
